Same return, different tax: how interest, Canadian dividends and capital gains from a fund change what you keep

Give five funds the same pre-tax return and change only how it arrives: interest, eligible Canadian dividends, capital gains realized each year, gains deferred until sale, or any of them inside a TFSA. Compare the tax, the growth lost to early tax and the after-tax return.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the same fund return paid as interest, dividends, realized gains or deferred growth

Each fund starts with $50,000 and earns the same 6% a year before tax; only the form in which the return arrives changes. The combined marginal rate is 29.65% (20.5% federal plus 9.15% provincial or territorial). Interest is taxed at that rate, a realized capital gain at half of it, and an eligible dividend is grossed up by 38% and then reduced by the federal credit of 15.0198% and the entered provincial credit, both measured on the grossed-up amount. Income is taxed in the year paid and the after-tax cash is reinvested; unrealized growth is taxed only on the sale at the horizon. Returns are constant hypothetical inputs, not forecasts or the record of any fund, and this is not a personal tax calculation.

The central idea

In a non-registered account, the form of a fund’s return matters as much as its size. Interest is taxed fully every year, eligible Canadian dividends receive a credit, realized gains are half included, and unrealized gains wait until a sale. A TFSA removes the difference. None of this makes a fund tax-exempt or its returns certain.

01

A fund passes its income through to you, and the label on that income sets the tax

A mutual fund or ETF held in a non-registered account is not taxed as one lump. CRA’s guidance on mutual funds explains that the interest, dividends and capital gains a fund distributes are reported by the investor in the year they are paid, even when they are reinvested in more units. Growth that stays inside the unit price is not taxed until the units are sold. The same 6% return can therefore produce very different tax bills depending on whether it arrives as interest, as Canadian dividends, as capital gains distributions or as a rising unit price.

This guide holds the pre-tax return fixed and changes only its form. That separates two questions that are often blurred: how much a fund earns, which nobody knows in advance, and how the account and the type of income are taxed, which follows published rules. A fund is never tax-exempt on its own; the tax result belongs to the account and the investor.

02

Three sets of rules for three kinds of income

The first chart shows the tax on CAD 100 of each kind of income at the default combined marginal rate of 29.65%: the 2026 federal rate of 20.5% on income from CAD 58,523 to CAD 117,045, plus Ontario’s 9.15% second-bracket rate, both from CRA’s 2026 rate table. These defaults are an example, not a recommendation of a province or a description of your bracket.

  • Interest is fully taxable: CAD 29.65 of tax on CAD 100.
  • Eligible Canadian dividends are grossed up: CRA’s instructions multiply the amount received by 138%, so CAD 100 becomes CAD 138 of taxable income. The federal dividend tax credit is 15.0198% of that grossed-up amount, about CAD 20.73, and Ontario’s 2025 worksheet applies 10% of the grossed-up amount, CAD 13.80. Net tax is about CAD 6.39.
  • A realized capital gain is half included, as CRA’s capital gains guidance shows, so CAD 100 adds CAD 50 of taxable income and about CAD 14.83 of tax.
  • Inside a TFSA, CRA says interest, dividends and capital gains are generally tax-free, including on withdrawal.

The dividend credit is designed to account for tax already paid by the corporation. It applies to dividends from taxable Canadian corporations; foreign dividends are taxed like interest and may have foreign tax withheld.

03

Twenty years later, the gap is mostly lost compounding

Each fund starts with CAD 50,000 and earns 6% a year before tax for 20 years. Income is taxed in the year it is paid and the after-tax amount is reinvested. At the end, the non-registered units are sold and any remaining gain is taxed.

  • Interest-paying fund: about CAD 114,308 after tax, an after-tax return of about 4.22% a year.
  • High-turnover fund, with all growth realized each year as capital gains distributions: about CAD 135,485, or 5.11% a year.
  • Low-turnover fund, with all growth deferred until the sale: about CAD 143,996, or 5.43%.
  • Canadian dividend fund paying 3% in eligible dividends with 3% price growth: about CAD 146,642, or 5.53%.
  • Any of these inside a TFSA: about CAD 160,357, the full 6%.

The third chart reconciles each bar to the TFSA value. For the interest fund, about CAD 27,103 went to yearly tax and about CAD 18,946 is growth those tax payments would have earned had they stayed invested. The low-turnover fund pays no yearly tax and loses no compounding; its whole cost, about CAD 16,360, falls due at the sale. That is why deferral matters: the tax is not smaller in rate, but the money stays at work longer.

04

The ranking changes with the tax bracket

At the default middle-bracket rates, eligible dividends are taxed more lightly than even a deferred capital gain. That does not hold everywhere. Using the top 2026 federal rate of 33% and Ontario’s top rate of 13.16%, the eligible-dividend rate rises to about 29.17% against 23.08% for capital gains. With those inputs the low-turnover fund ends at about CAD 134,886, ahead of the dividend fund at about CAD 124,255, while the interest fund falls to about CAD 94,433.

In the lowest brackets the dividend credits can exceed the tax on the grossed-up amount. With 14% federal and Ontario’s 5.05%, the model shows a negative dividend rate of about −8.24%: each CAD 100 of eligible dividends reduces tax on other income by about CAD 8.24. The credits are non-refundable, so that only works if there is other tax to reduce. The gross-up also raises net income, which can increase the OAS recovery tax or reduce income-tested benefits; the OAS recovery guide shows how that clawback is calculated. Use your own province’s Form 428 rates before drawing a conclusion.

05

Higher returns widen the gap; they do not change its direction

The heatmap repeats the 20-year comparison for pre-tax returns from 3% to 8%. At 3%, the interest fund keeps about 2.11% a year and the TFSA 3%. At 8%, the interest fund keeps about 5.63% and the TFSA 8%. The tax drag in percentage points grows with the return, because tax takes a share of every dollar of income.

A fund’s income mix is not fixed. Bond funds pay mostly interest. Canadian equity funds often pay eligible dividends but may also distribute capital gains when the manager sells holdings. Index funds and ETFs with low turnover usually realize fewer gains, but can still distribute some. Fund Facts, annual reports and past tax slips show what a fund has paid; past distributions do not guarantee future ones, and a fund that changes its holdings can change its tax character.

06

Do not choose a fund for its tax label alone

A fund that is tax-efficient can still be a poor fit. A Canadian dividend fund concentrates in one country and often in a few sectors, such as banks, energy and utilities. A bond fund that pays fully taxable interest may be the part of a balanced portfolio that falls least in an equity crash. Diversification, risk tolerance, time horizon and fees usually matter more than the difference between tax rates on income types.

Several things the model leaves out can change the answer: a sale large enough to push income into a higher bracket, capital losses that can offset gains, return of capital distributions that lower the adjusted cost base, foreign withholding tax, and provincial surtaxes or health premiums. The fund cost-base guide traces return of capital, and the gain-timing guide compares realizing gains every year with one final sale.

07

Using the tax rules without letting them drive the plan

  1. Choose the investment mix first: what share in equities, bonds and cash you can hold through a decline.
  2. Use registered room where it fits. A TFSA removes the tax difference between income types; an RRSP defers tax but taxes withdrawals as ordinary income, so dividends and gains lose their lower rates there. The RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares the two.
  3. If both registered and non-registered accounts hold funds, the asset-location guide tests which fund to shelter first.
  4. Distinguish contributions from your paycheque, which add to all accounts over time, from moving an existing non-registered holding, which can realize a capital gain when sold or transferred in kind.
  5. Keep records of reinvested distributions; they raise your adjusted cost base and reduce the gain reported on a later sale.
  6. Have a tax professional review a large reorganization. This guide explains mechanics and is not tax advice.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The 38% gross-up, the 15.0198% federal dividend tax credit, the one-half capital gains inclusion rate and the 2026 federal and Ontario rates used as defaults are dated CRA figures. Fund returns, dividend yields, balances and holding periods are hypothetical editable inputs, not forecasts, fund data or a personal tax calculation. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
